title: King Charles Marks the British Asian Trust's 20th Year With a £1 Million Gala. The Timing Is Not Coincidental.
excerpt: The monarch's charity has supported 18.8 million people across South Asia. At a London gala held against the backdrop of anti-Asian unrest, his presence sent a pointed message about community and belonging.
body:
King Charles III stepped into the Peninsula London earlier this week for the kind of event that might, in quieter times, have been a straightforward celebration: the annual dinner and reception of the British Asian Trust, the charity he founded in 2007 as Prince of Wales after a charity cricket match between India and Pakistan.

This was not a quieter time. The gala, which raised more than £1 million in a single evening, came against the backdrop of sectarian violence in Belfast, where homes and businesses belonging to ethnic minorities have been attacked in recent weeks. In parts of England, tensions remain high following the murder of a university student by a Sikh man — an incident that has been exploited by far-right groups to fuel anti-Asian sentiment.

Dame Meera Syal, the actress and writer who received her damehood from the King just a week earlier at Windsor Castle, said the monarch's continued involvement felt "very much" significant given the timing.

"We're incredibly thrilled that we still have his patronage and that the Trust is going from strength to strength," she told the Press Association. "And I think, especially in times like this, to celebrate communities coming together and unity is really important."

## Two Decades of Quiet Impact

The British Asian Trust was born from an unusual moment: Charles, then the heir to the throne, watching Rahul Dravid and Shoaib Malik lead their teams in a charity cricket match. At the gala, Vice-Chairs Asif Rangoonwala and Shalni Arora presented the King with a framed photograph from that 2007 game — a memento that traced the arc from a sporting afternoon to a development organisation that has now reached 18.8 million people across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka.

The charity's work spans child protection, education, mental health, livelihoods, and environmental conservation. It specialises in social finance — using market-based instruments to fund development in South Asia — and has become a prominent vehicle for the British Asian diaspora to channel philanthropy back to the region.

"We are grateful for the continued interest our Royal Founding Patron, His Majesty the King, takes in the Trust's work," said Hitan Mehta, the Trust's CEO, who was awarded an OBE by Charles for services to the British Asian community two years ago.

"Tonight, we also celebrate the extraordinary impact being delivered across South Asia, made possible by the commitment and generosity of the British Asian diaspora and our wider partners."

## A Signal in a Difficult Moment

What made the evening resonate beyond the charity circuit was the political context. In Belfast, an Indian woman named Ruchira Rangaprasad — who moved to Northern Ireland three years ago — has been providing home-cooked meals to families too afraid to leave their homes after racist attacks. More than 30 volunteers, most of them strangers, stepped forward to help her distribute food boxes.

The contrast between these acts of community solidarity and the violence that necessitated them hangs over any celebration of the British Asian community's contributions to the UK. Lord Jitesh Gadhia, chair of the British Asian Trust, acknowledged the broader significance.

"This year marks a particularly special milestone as we begin celebrating the Trust's 20th anniversary," he said. "And the work is far from complete."

The gala evening included a performance by British R&B singer Jay Sean and was sponsored by Westcombe Group, OakNorth, and Godwit Travel. Funds raised will support programmes across South Asia — a reminder that the diaspora's relationship with the subcontinent is not merely sentimental but actively generative.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the 1.9 million people of Indian origin living in the United Kingdom, the King's continued patronage of a charity explicitly built around the British Asian identity carries weight that goes beyond philanthropy. At a moment when politicians are debating immigration, integration, and the limits of multiculturalism, the head of state choosing to spend his evening celebrating the community's contributions is, as Dame Meera put it, "very much" a deliberate gesture.

The British Asian Trust will formally mark its 20th anniversary in 2027. If the current trajectory holds — both the charity's growth and the political climate it operates in — that celebration may carry even more freight than this one.
